name: Martin Luther
role: Augustinian friar, professor of theology, reformer

born.place: Eisleben, County of Mansfeld, Holy Roman Empire

died.cause: Illness, probably heart failure, after years of poor health

summary: German friar and professor whose challenge to the sale of indulgences in 1517 sparked the Protestant Reformation and whose German Bible shaped both the church and the German language.

key_dates.label: Caught in a thunderstorm, vows to become a monk; enters the Augustinian friary at Erfurt
Receives doctorate in theology; becomes professor at Wittenberg
Writes the Ninety-five Theses against indulgences (31 October)
Publishes three major reform treatises; burns the papal bull
Excommunicated; refuses to recant at the Diet of Worms
Publishes his German New Testament ("September Testament")

accomplishments.text: Wrote the Ninety-five Theses (1517) disputing the sale of indulgences, which spread rapidly by printing and started the Reformation.
Taught that sinners are justified before God by grace through faith alone, not by works or purchased merit.
In 1520 published To the Christian Nobility of the German Nation, The Babylonian Captivity of the Church, and The Freedom of a Christian.
Refused to recant his writings before Emperor Charles V at the Diet of Worms (April 1521) unless convinced by Scripture and plain reason.
Translated the New Testament into German while hidden at the Wartburg castle (published 1522), and with colleagues completed the whole Bible by 1534.
Married the former nun Katharina von Bora (1525), modeling a married Protestant clergy.
Wrote The Bondage of the Will (1525) in reply to Erasmus on free will and grace.
Wrote the Small and Large Catechisms (1529) for teaching families and pastors, and many hymns including "A Mighty Fortress Is Our God."

persecution_note: Luther was condemned as a heretic by the pope and declared an outlaw by the emperor, but he was never arrested or executed. Princes who protected him kept him out of reach, and he died of natural causes in 1546. Some of his followers were executed.

persecution.title: Heresy proceedings in Rome; examined at Augsburg
persecution.summary: Archbishop Albrecht of Mainz, whose indulgence campaign Luther had attacked, sent the Ninety-five Theses to Rome, and the papal court opened a heresy case. Luther was summoned to Rome. Instead, at the request of his prince, he was examined at Augsburg in October 1518 by the papal legate, Cardinal Cajetan, who demanded that he recant. Luther refused and left the city secretly at night.

responsible.name: Albrecht of Brandenburg
responsible.role: Archbishop of Mainz; reported the theses to Rome

responsible.name: Sylvester Prierias
responsible.role: Master of the Sacred Palace (papal theologian); wrote the official reply calling his views heretical

responsible.name: Cardinal Thomas Cajetan
responsible.role: Papal legate; examined him at Augsburg and demanded recantation

defended_by.name: Frederick the Wise
defended_by.role: Elector of Saxony; refused to send him to Rome

persecution.outcome: Luther did not recant, and he stayed in Saxony under Frederick's protection.

persecution.title: Condemned by the papal bull Exsurge Domine; books burned
persecution.summary: In June 1520 Pope Leo X issued the bull Exsurge Domine. It condemned 41 statements from Luther's writings, ordered his books burned, and gave him 60 days to recant or face excommunication. Johann Eck, who had helped prepare it, and the papal nuncio Girolamo Aleander published it in Germany, and Luther's books were burned at Louvain, Cologne, and Mainz.

responsible.name: Johann Eck
responsible.role: Theologian; helped prepare the bull and published it in Germany
responsible.jurisdiction: University of Ingolstadt; acting as papal agent

responsible.name: Girolamo Aleander
responsible.role: Papal nuncio; organized the burning of Luther's books

persecution.outcome: Luther publicly burned the bull and the books of canon law at Wittenberg on 10 December 1520.

persecution.title: Excommunicated
persecution.summary: Pope Leo X formally excommunicated Luther in the bull Decet Romanum Pontificem.

persecution.title: Declared an outlaw by the Edict of Worms
persecution.summary: After Luther refused to recant at the Diet of Worms, Emperor Charles V issued the Edict of Worms, drafted by the papal nuncio Aleander. It placed Luther under the imperial ban, forbade anyone to shelter him, ordered his arrest, and banned his writings. Frederick the Wise had him taken to the Wartburg castle in a staged kidnapping, to hide him.

responsible.name: Diet of Worms
responsible.role: Imperial assembly before which he was tried; the estates accepted the edict

defended_by.name: Frederick the Wise
defended_by.role: Elector of Saxony; hid him at the Wartburg (1521–1522) and never enforced the edict

persecution.outcome: Luther lived under the imperial ban for the rest of his life, but it was never enforced in Saxony, and he was never arrested.

persecution.title: His New Testament banned in Catholic territories
persecution.summary: Catholic rulers banned Luther's German New Testament in their lands. In neighboring Ducal (Albertine) Saxony, Duke George ordered copies surrendered and punished people who kept them.

responsible.name: Duke George of Saxony
responsible.role: Ruler of Ducal Saxony; banned the translation

persecution.outcome: The translation spread anyway and went through many printings.

persecution.title: First of his followers burned: Voes and van den Esschen
persecution.summary: Hendrik Voes and Johann van den Esschen, Augustinian friars from Antwerp who held Luther's teachings, were burned for heresy in Brussels. They were the first people executed as Lutherans. Luther wrote his first hymn, "A New Song Here Shall Be Begun," about their deaths.

responsible.name: Inquisitors in the Habsburg Netherlands
responsible.role: Tried and condemned them for heresy
responsible.jurisdiction: Habsburg Netherlands, under Emperor Charles V

responsible.name: Government of the Habsburg Netherlands
responsible.jurisdiction: Habsburg Netherlands, under Emperor Charles V

excommunication_note: Luther was excommunicated once, by Pope Leo X in 1521, after he refused to recant within the 60 days the pope had given him in 1520. The sentence was never lifted.

excommunications.reason: Refused to recant the 41 statements condemned in Exsurge Domine (June 1520), and publicly burned that bull

persecuted_others_note: Luther at first argued that heresy should be fought with the word, not with fire (1523), and in 1528 lamented the burning of Anabaptists. Later he urged the princes to kill the rebelling peasants (1525), endorsed memoranda supporting the death penalty for Anabaptists (1531, 1536), and in 1543 called on rulers to burn synagogues and expel or subjugate the Jews, reversing his conciliatory tract of 1523.

persecuted_others.title: Against the Robbing and Murdering Hordes of Peasants
persecuted_others.targets: Rebelling peasants in the German Peasants' War
persecuted_others.summary: In May 1525 Luther urged the princes to "smite, slay, and stab" the rebels, whom he regarded as rebels against God-given authority. The killing was carried out by the princes' armies, including those of Philip of Hesse and Duke George of Saxony at Frankenhausen; Luther defended his tract later that year in An Open Letter on the Harsh Book.
persecuted_others.outcome: The revolt was crushed; tens of thousands of peasants were killed (the often-quoted estimate is about 100,000).

persecuted_others.title: Endorsed the death penalty for Anabaptists
persecuted_others.summary: Luther added his approval to a 1531 memorandum by Philip Melanchthon holding that Anabaptists who refused to recant could be put to death, and in 1536 he signed a Wittenberg memorandum (written by Melanchthon for Philip of Hesse) supporting the death penalty for Anabaptist leaders and for those who defied banishment, treating their teaching as sedition and blasphemy. Philip of Hesse himself avoided executing Anabaptists.
persecuted_others.outcome: Anabaptists were executed in Electoral Saxony in this period.

persecuted_others.title: On the Jews and Their Lies
persecuted_others.summary: Luther urged rulers to set fire to synagogues and Jewish schools, destroy Jewish homes, take away prayer books and Talmudic writings, forbid rabbis to teach, deny Jews safe conduct, ban usury, and put them to manual labor, or else expel them. He repeated these themes in other 1543 tracts and in an admonition against the Jews appended to his last sermon in 1546. Earlier, in 1537, he had declined to intercede for Jews expelled from Electoral Saxony.
persecuted_others.outcome: Few rulers adopted his program at the time, but the tract was later republished and cited by Nazi propagandists; Lutheran church bodies have since repudiated it.
